title: Long-Term Mental Health Consequences of Being Arrested on Arrestees and Their Families

content_html_sanitized:
Every few days we hear about the “latest research” that purports to warn about what the dire consequences of using cannabis may be, but we almost never hear about the number of arrests for marijuana offenses, or the adverse consequences of being arrested.

 

Well, I hate to tell you this, but being arrested isn’t harmless, the way we all thought back in the sixties.

Pardon the sarcasm.

 

For over thirty years I have been complaining about the mass media’s failure to inform the American people about the number of marijuana arrests.

 

In the last fifty years police have made an estimated 30 million arrests, peaking at over 870,000  in 2007, and still continuing at over 200,000 per year, Over eighty five per cent are for simple possession.

 

Obviously, some of the arrests are repeat offenders, but a number of arrests go unreported.

 

In any case, the adverse effects of so many mostly young men, disproportionately from racial minorities, has a significant social, economic and public health impact.

 

For context, the following is from MarijuanaNews.com’s 1998 Frequently Asked Questions, and then to keep up with the times, I decided to ask Chat GPT about the health consequences of being arrested.

From MarijuanaNews.com Frequently Asked Questions from 1998:

“If you have made it this far into this site you probably already know that there have been almost eleven million marijuana arrests in the last thirty years. Presently, there is another arrest every 54 seconds or so. This is a rate of over half a million per year. Roughly eighty-five percent of these are for simple possession.

Don't be embarrassed, though, if you did not know this. Eric Schlosser, the author of three major articles in The Atlantic Monthly More Reefer Madness about marijuana prohibition, began his first article in 1994 by relating that this very question was asked by the editors of the magazine at the beginning of their discussions about the article. If these exceptionally well-informed people do not know, then why should anyone?

The fact is that the arrest numbers are almost never reported.

 

Since NORML first started trying to publicize the numbers in 1993, they have been reported only once to my knowledge. This February, Bernard Shaw of CNN related the arrest numbers at the end of a special about marijuana, and even gave NORML as the source. Unprecedented and unduplicated.

 

The fact that no one knows these numbers allows the prohibitionists to claim that not enough is being done to "fight marijuana," and to ignore the costs of prohibition. The Clinton Administration's failure to cite these numbers in its own defense when it is being accused of being "soft on marijuana" is one of the most curious aspects of this silence. When the total arrests pass the eleven million mark this year, anti-prohibitionists should demand that the media report these numbers.

 

As for what happens when someone is arrested, the consequences range from minor embarrassment to having their lives ruined. Obviously, much depends on who you are and where you get caught. Congressman Dan Burton's son has been caught twice with large quantities of marijuana and nothing happened to him. In his most recent Atlantic article Schlosser talks about people who have gotten life sentences for a joint. Of course, prison is not all that can happen to someone.

 

In "lenient" California someone arrested in their home can lose their driver's license, which can obviously mean the loss of a job. In other places people can lose custody of their children. If a person is charged with cultivation of just one plant, the consequences can be even more dire. People can and do lose their homes, farms, etc. to "civil forfeiture."

 

For medical marijuana users the consequences can be even worse.

They can be deprived of the only medicine that has given them relief from their suffering and then be forced to take pharmaceuticals that leave them debilitated and yet not help them.

 

This is analogous to the Soviet's abuse of its political dissidents by imprisoning them in psychiatric hospitals and forcing them to take drugs that threatened their sanity. We treat our more numerous pharmaceutical dissidents even more cruelly.

 

The variation in the consequences of getting arrested on a marijuana charge is one of the injustices of marijuana prohibition that can only be addressed by publicizing the arrest statistics and the consequences of arrests. Inasmuch as this might undermine public support for marijuana prohibition, these facts are pro-drug and anti-child and therefore must be consigned to the memory hole. Now that you know them, you must eat your computer.”

 

From Chat GPT. Sources below.

“While the adverse mental health effects of imprisonment are well documented, research now shows that the act of being arrested itself can have significant long-term mental health repercussions . The trauma, stress, and social consequences associated with an arrest can affect not only the individual, but also ripple out to their family members. This report examines these long-term mental health outcomes – including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, chronic stress, and social stigma – on arrested individuals, and explores the collateral impacts on their families (emotional distress, economic hardship, intergenerational trauma, and shifts in family dynamics). The findings draw on U.S.-based psychological, sociological, and public health research.

Mental Health Consequences for Arrested Individuals

Arrest and other forms of criminal justice contact are strongly linked to poorer mental health outcomes. In fact, one longitudinal study found that arrest alone is responsible for nearly half of the association between incarceration and subsequent mental health problems . Arrested persons often face immediate stressors such as social stigma, feelings of powerlessness and alienation, burdensome legal processes, and uncertainty about the future – all of which can damage mental health . Below we detail key long-term mental health outcomes observed among individuals who have been arrested.

Depression and Mood Disorders

A history of arrest or incarceration is associated with elevated rates of depression and other mood disorders. Research shows incarceration is linked to mood disorders including major depressive disorder , and even “less intensive” contacts like arrest can deleteriously affect mental health . A comprehensive review of U.S. data found that all forms of criminalization tend to negatively impact mental health, contributing to higher levels of depressive symptoms and even suicidal ideation . In practical terms, this means that individuals who have been arrested are at greater risk of persistent sadness, hopelessness, and clinical depression long after the legal events. For example, one study noted that even after controlling for other factors, people who had experienced an arrest reported significantly more depressive symptoms than those with no justice system contact . In the long run, untreated depression can impede these individuals’ ability to reintegrate into society, maintain employment, and build healthy relationships.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and Trauma

Being arrested – especially if the incident involves violence, harsh conditions, or perceived injustice – can be a profoundly traumatic event. Incarceration researchers have even identified a pattern of post-release symptoms termed “Post-Incarceration Syndrome,” a syndrome similar to PTSD in its clinical presentation . Many people exposed to jail or prison report classic PTSD symptoms such as anxiety, hyper-vigilance, flashbacks, nightmares, and avoidance behaviors . A 2019 literature review revealed that incarcerated individuals are frequently exposed to potentially traumatic events (PTEs) behind bars, and experiencing more of these traumas was strongly correlated with higher rates of PTSD upon release . In other words, the more trauma a person endures during arrest or incarceration, the more likely they are to suffer lasting PTSD symptoms . These symptoms can persist for years, causing individuals to relive the distress of their arrest or confinement. It’s worth noting that pre-existing trauma can be both a cause and consequence of criminal justice involvement: one study found that people with extensive trauma histories (or pre-existing PTSD) were more likely to be arrested in the first place . Once in the system, however, the cycle continues, as new traumatic experiences (such as aggressive arrest tactics or violence in detention) compound their psychological harm. Long after the legal case is over, individuals may remain trapped in a state of fight-or-flight, struggling with PTSD alongside other mental health challenges.

Anxiety Disorders and Chronic Stress

Alongside depression, anxiety disorders are a common long-term outcome for those who have been arrested or incarcerated. The stress of being handcuffed, detained, and facing possible prosecution can trigger intense fear and anxiety in the moment – and for some, that anxiety does not simply resolve after release. Population studies find that exposure to the criminal legal system is linked to elevated anxiety levels . For instance, one nationally representative survey showed that a first incarceration (often preceded by an arrest) was associated with new onset of anxiety disorders in previously healthy individuals . There are several reasons why arrest leads to chronic anxiety. First, the bureaucratic uncertainty – awaiting trial, dealing with court dates, or the possibility of future rearrest – can create ongoing worry and hyperarousal . Individuals often describe a persistent sense of being “on edge,” fearing unexpected knocks on the door or interactions with law enforcement. Second, an arrest record can introduce long-term instability in one’s life (loss of employment opportunities, housing difficulties, etc.), contributing to chronic stress that feeds anxiety. Finally, the social and self-stigma of having been arrested can cause people to feel constant judgment or surveillance, again heightening anxiety. Physiologically, this chronic stress from the post-arrest fallout keeps the body’s stress response activated, which is harmful to mental health. Over time, chronic stress can manifest as generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks, sleep disturbances, and other stress-related disorders. Indeed, researchers have characterized involvement with the justice system as a serious chronic stressor that can “exacerbate minority health inequalities” by adding to the cumulative stress burden in disadvantaged communities . In summary, being arrested often kicks off a prolonged period of uncertainty and tension in an individual’s life, leading to entrenched anxiety and stress-related health problems.

Social Stigma and Isolation

Social stigma is another less tangible but powerful mental health consequence of being arrested. Individuals labeled as “arrestees,” “ex-cons,” or “criminals” frequently experience public shame and discrimination that can impede their social functioning and self-esteem. As noted by criminology researchers, arrested people face social stigma, feelings of powerlessness and alienation during and after the criminal justice process . This stigma can take many forms: former defendants may lose friends, be treated with suspicion by neighbors or employers, or face judgment even from family members. Such societal reactions can lead the individual to withdraw and become socially isolated. Research in mental health shows that social isolation and alienation worsen psychological well-being, often leading to or aggravating depression and chronic stress . Moreover, having a criminal record (even for an arrest without conviction) poses structural barriers – for example, background checks can limit job and housing prospects – which reinforces the sense of being an “outsider” in one’s own community. The internalized stigma can be as damaging as external prejudice: many individuals feel deep shame or guilt about their arrest, which erodes their self-worth and can deter them from seeking help for mental health issues. In essence, the arrest becomes a label that overshadows their identity, causing social and psychological marginalization. Studies have pointed out that these experiences of powerlessness and uncertainty in the aftermath of an arrest are significant stressors on mental health . Thus, social stigma operates as both a direct source of emotional pain and an indirect driver of other mental health problems, creating a vicious cycle that can be hard to break without support.

Impacts on Families of Arrested Individuals

The consequences of an arrest extend beyond the individual; they profoundly affect families as well. When a family member is arrested (and possibly incarcerated), loved ones left behind often experience a cascade of emotional, economic, and social challenges. In the United States, family member incarceration has become distressingly common – one estimate in 2021 concluded that having an incarcerated family member is “now common for American families” and that it has negative effects on families above and beyond any preexisting disadvantages . Approximately one in 14 U.S. children (7%) has had a parent incarcerated at some point during childhood , highlighting how widespread this issue is. This section examines the long-term impacts on family members, including psychological distress, financial strain, intergenerational trauma, and shifts in family dynamics.

Emotional and Psychological Distress in Families

Families of arrested individuals often suffer significant emotional turmoil. The sudden loss of a parent, spouse, or child to the justice system can be experienced as a form of family crisis or grief. Partners and caregivers (disproportionately women, given the majority of inmates are men) commonly report elevated levels of stress, anxiety, and depression when their loved one is behind bars . In fact, a review of health impacts of incarceration noted that having a family member incarcerated has profound effects on the health and well-being of the adult women left behind . These women frequently become solo caregivers and face the emotional burden of worrying about the safety and fate of their incarcerated loved one. Studies have documented “maternal distress” in such situations – for example, mothers whose partners are incarcerated show higher rates of depressive symptoms and chronic stress, even after accounting for socio-economic factors that existed beforehand .

Children and other relatives also experience emotional distress. Many children feel confusion, anger, sadness, or shame about a parent’s arrest. The event of witnessing a parental arrest can itself be traumatic: one study found that children under age 8 who actually saw their parent being arrested showed significantly higher internalizing problems (like anxiety and withdrawal) and externalizing problems (acting out) for months afterward . Even older children and teenagers, who might not articulate it, often endure chronic worry and embarrassment about their parent’s situation. The entire family can be plunged into a state of chronic emotional strain, sometimes comparable to the stress of a death in the family. However, unlike death, incarceration carries stigma – families may hesitate to seek community support or may receive less sympathy, exacerbating their isolation. The shame or social stigma by association can weigh heavily on families, as one report noted: children of incarcerated parents often experience feelings of shame and social stigma, weakened attachment, and a sense of abandonment . This emotional strain on families can have lasting implications, contributing to mental health issues such as depression or PTSD among family members and potentially straining familial relationships even after the incarcerated member returns home.

Economic Hardship and Financial Strain

One of the most immediate and long-lasting impacts on families is economic hardship following an arrest or incarceration of a loved one. Many individuals who get arrested are breadwinners or contributors to family income; their removal can create a sudden loss of earnings. Additionally, families often incur significant costs related to legal fees, bail, court fines, and maintaining contact (e.g., expensive prison phone calls or travel for visitation). A major national survey in 2015 exposed the steep financial toll on families: Nearly 65% of families with an incarcerated member were unable to meet basic needs like food and housing because of the costs of incarceration . On average, families in the survey incurred over $13,000 in court-related debts and fees due to their loved one’s conviction – an enormous burden, especially considering that many affected families were low-income to begin with. In 63% of cases, family members (predominantly women) on the outside had to bear these costs , often forcing difficult trade-offs like skipping utility bills or rent to pay legal expenses.

This financial stress can persist for years, even after the arrested individual has served their sentence. Families may deplete savings, go into debt, or face credit problems due to unpaid fines. The loss of one income combined with added expenses can push families into poverty or homelessness. Economic hardship and mental health are closely intertwined – persistent financial strain is known to increase risks of depression, anxiety, and toxic stress in caregivers. Indeed, research has shown that economic hardship has an adverse impact on mental health of family members . Caregivers juggling multiple jobs or extra hours to compensate for lost income may experience burnout. In some cases, older children or grandparents must step into caretaking or earning roles, which can disrupt their own education or retirement. Overall, the arrest of a family member often forces the entire household into a prolonged period of economic instability, which itself becomes a chronic stressor layered on top of the emotional pain. This combination of money problems and emotional strain can create a vicious cycle, whereby financial difficulties worsen family members’ mental health, and mental distress (like depression) in turn makes it harder to cope and climb out of economic hardship.

Intergenerational Trauma and Children’s Outcomes

Arrests can set in motion intergenerational effects, impacting the mental health and well-being of children for years or even decades. Parental arrest/incarceration is now recognized as a significant Adverse Childhood Experience (ACE) – an early life trauma that can have long-term health consequences. Children of incarcerated parents are an extremely vulnerable group, showing much higher rates of mental health and behavioral problems than their peers . In particular, having a parent in jail or prison is associated with markedly higher risks of depression, anxiety, and behavioral issues in childhood. In one nationally representative study, children with an incarcerated parent were over three times more likely to suffer from depression or behavioral problems compared to otherwise similar children without an incarcerated parent . They were also about twice as likely to develop anxiety disorders or attention problems . This shows how a parent’s incarceration can compound the adversity in a child’s life, leading to emotional dysregulation, sadness, and acting-out behaviors. Young children may experience the parent’s absence as a form of attachment trauma, sometimes exhibiting symptoms akin to separation anxiety or PTSD. For example, as mentioned earlier, witnessing a parent’s arrest is an acute trauma that can instill fear and anxiety in a child, affecting their behavior and mental state long after the event .

The trauma of parental incarceration often continues to reverberate into adolescence and adulthood. Longitudinal research by public health experts at the CDC found that exposure to parental incarceration in childhood was significantly associated with multiple mental health problems in young adulthood, including depression, PTSD, and anxiety disorders . In that study, individuals who had a parent imprisoned during their youth had 1.4 to 1.7 times higher odds of major depression, PTSD, and anxiety in their late teens and twenties, compared to those with no such history . This suggests an intergenerational transmission of trauma and stress: the hardships endured in childhood set the stage for future mental health struggles. Other research similarly indicates that parental incarceration can contribute to long-term issues like difficulty forming trusting relationships, lower educational attainment, and even higher risk of the children themselves becoming involved in the criminal justice system, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as the cycle of intergenerational criminal justice involvement . In essence, the child’s trauma and social disadvantage may translate into behavioral problems or survival strategies that increase their likelihood of later arrest, continuing the cycle.

It’s important to note that parental incarceration is often compared to losing a parent through death or divorce in terms of its impact on a child . However, in some ways it can be more complex: the child may hold onto hope of reunification, yet face uncertainty and sporadic contact, which can be psychologically confusing. They may also face stigma (being bullied or socially ostracized due to a parent in prison), compounding their trauma with shame. Without intervention and support (counseling, mentoring, etc.), many of these children carry forward the emotional scars of their parent’s arrest. This intergenerational trauma underlines why the effects of an arrest are not confined to one person – they can extend into the next generation’s mental health and life chances.

Changes in Family Dynamics

When a member of a family is arrested and especially if they are incarcerated for a time, the entire family system undergoes change. These changes in family dynamics can themselves be a source of stress and long-term dysfunction. One immediate effect is family structure disruption: if a parent is removed from the household, the family often has to reorganize roles and responsibilities. For instance, the remaining parent (or a grandparent) suddenly becomes a single caregiver; older children might need to take on adult responsibilities (childcare for younger siblings, working part-time, etc.). This can alter parent-child relationships and sibling relationships. The literature on this topic shows that immediate effects on children include weakened ties to the incarcerated parent and changes in family composition (such as moving homes or living with relatives) . There may also be a loss of parental authority – a parent who is absent cannot discipline or guide as before, which can lead children to question or resent their authority once the parent returns . Moreover, caregivers left behind might change household rules or routines under stress, leading to confusion or conflict among family members.

Another aspect is the strain on family bonds and marital relationships. Maintaining relationships through the bars of a jail is challenging; many couples struggle to sustain intimacy and trust during incarceration. Regular family activities – eating together, celebrating holidays – are interrupted, which can weaken the emotional bonds. It is telling that more than half of incarcerated parents in one survey reported never receiving a visit from their children while in prison , often due to distance or cost. This lack of contact can lead to feelings of abandonment on both sides. Even when contact is maintained via calls or letters, it is a far cry from daily interaction, and children especially may feel a mix of loyalty and estrangement. By the time the incarcerated family member returns, the family’s routines and hierarchy may have shifted significantly, making reunification stressful. Long-term, some families never fully recover their prior stability – the risk of family dissolution or divorce increases with incarceration, and some children remain in the care of alternate guardians even after the parent’s release.

Additionally, families often grapple with role confusion and identity changes. A child might feel they have “lost” the image of a protective father or nurturing mother if that parent is in jail, altering the child’s sense of security. Spouses might oscillate between the role of a loyal partner and a practically single individual. Extended family members (like grandparents, aunts/uncles) might step in as caregivers, changing the family’s makeup and sometimes causing tension or differences in parenting styles. All these dynamic shifts require adjustment and can be psychologically taxing for everyone involved. Research has described how children of incarcerated parents often endure multiple placements or caregiving changes, leading to instability that can affect their development and trust in others . The cumulative effect of these family dynamic changes can be seen in some long-term outcomes: for example, youth with incarcerated parents have higher rates of school problems and delinquency, possibly stemming from the reduced parental supervision and altered family environment . Families, in short, are forced to adapt to a “new normal” in the absence of the arrested member, and this adaptation is frequently accompanied by stress, conflict, and grief.

Conclusion

Arrest is not a one-day event but a life-altering experience that can leave psychological scars on both individuals and their families. For the individual, an arrest can trigger enduring mental health challenges – from depression and PTSD to chronic anxiety and social withdrawal – that persist long after the case is resolved. The social stigma attached to arrest further compounds these issues by isolating individuals and limiting their opportunities for recovery and reintegration . At the same time, families bear a hidden share of the burden. Loved ones left behind often experience intense emotional distress, ranging from the acute trauma of a witnessed arrest to the chronic sadness of an absent family member. Many families are pushed into financial hardship by legal costs and lost income, a stressor that feeds back into mental health strain . Children, arguably the most innocent parties, can suffer intergenerational trauma that affects their developmental trajectory and emotional well-being well into adulthood . And as family roles and dynamics shift to cope with the loss, relationships may fracture or take years to mend .

These findings underscore that the impact of the criminal justice system cannot be measured solely by incarceration rates or crime statistics – there is a profound public health and social dimension to consider. Each arrest sets off a ripple effect: a mental health crisis for the individual, and collateral damage for spouses, children, and communities. Importantly, these outcomes are not distributed evenly. Communities of color and low-income populations, who experience higher rates of arrest, also bear a disproportionate burden of these mental health and family impacts , thereby widening existing health disparities. Recognizing the long-term consequences of arrest should inform policy and practice: it highlights the need for trauma-informed approaches in policing and courts, mental health support services for arrestees (e.g. counseling, diversion programs), and resources for families (such as support groups, financial assistance, and programs for children of incarcerated parents). By addressing these collateral consequences, we can mitigate some of the chronic depression, PTSD, anxiety, and familial distress that currently follow in the wake of an arrest. Ultimately, helping individuals and families heal and remain stable is not only a matter of compassion but also contributes to breaking cycles of trauma and reducing future involvement with the justice system.”

The Urban Institute (Travis et al., 2005) noted children of incarcerated parents often experience shame, stigma, loss of financial support, and weakened family bonds, with potential long-term developmental consequences . These sources collectively paint a picture of arrest as a catalyst for enduring mental health challenges and familial hardships in the U.S. context.
